descriptionChirho: To see with the eyes, the basic act of visual perception in any tense, person, or number, including aorist eidon, perfect heoraka, and present blepo-suppletive forms. The dominant sense across the NT with 419+ occurrences covering physical sight of persons, events, and objects. Multilingual glosses consistently render with visual-perception verbs: Arabic ra'a/yara, German sehen, French voir, Hebrew ra'ah, Hindi dekhna, Korean boda, Spanish ver.

Imperative or exclamatory use calling attention to something, functioning as an interjection meaning 'behold!' or 'look!', typically idou. With 256+ occurrences, this is the second most common use, found throughout the Gospels, Acts, and Revelation (Matt 1:20, 23; 2:1, 9, 13; Luke 1:31; Rev 1:7). Glosses: Arabic idha/ha, German siehe, French voir, Hebrew hinneh, Hindi dekho, Korean bora, Spanish he aqui.

Passive sense meaning to appear, become visible, or be seen, often of divine or supernatural manifestation. Used of Moses and Elijah appearing at the Transfiguration (Luke 9:31), tongues of fire appearing at Pentecost (Acts 2:3), the angel appearing to Moses in the burning bush (Acts 7:35), and the Lord appearing to Saul on the Damascus road (Acts 9:17). Hebrew glosses use nir'u (niphal of ra'ah), confirming the passive valence.

To perceive mentally or understand, grasping something with the mind rather than merely with the eyes. Used in prophetic quotations about spiritual blindness: 'seeing you will see and not perceive' (Matt 13:14; Mark 4:12; Acts 28:26, quoting Isa 6:9). The Hebrew gloss tede'u (from yada, 'to know') rather than tir'u (from ra'ah, 'to see') confirms the cognitive rather than visual sense.

To direct one's gaze intentionally toward something or someone, emphasizing the act of looking rather than mere sight. In John 19:37, 'They will look (opsontai) on him whom they pierced,' quoting Zech 12:10. The Hebrew gloss yabbitu (hiphil of nabat, 'to gaze intently') distinguishes this from ordinary seeing, and Spanish 'miraran' (from mirar, to look at) further confirms intentional directed gaze.
